title: Routing, risk labels and live metrics
bridge: Routing a review is like code splitting in a React app. A small page loads a small bundle, and a big page loads more. Except here the bundle is the model's effort and the review mode. And each route must prove on BYTE-GOLD that it still catches the bugs the expensive route catches.
intro: Today every Byte review runs Opus 5.5 at high effort, even a one-line docs fix. This lesson sizes each review to its PR. Effort follows size and kind, and a risk label tells the one reviewer where to look. A deep panel runs only where a miss hurts most. First, though, live numbers that show whether people act on Byte at all.

picture.caption: One PR event: the gate sizes the review and labels the risk; after the merge, each finding gets a fate.

nodes.label: riskFor: risk label and neutral check
the review: one session or the panel

steps.text: a PR event reaches Byte's gate
changed lines and kind pick low, medium or high effort

risk:high, more than 800 lines, or @byte-review deep means the panel
Byte reviews with that route and mode
after the merge, each finding is addressed or open, and wrong or not
nightly: addressed and wrong ratios per team; monthly: live recall

sections.h: Gold is fixed; live is real
p: BYTE-GOLD from lessons g2-1 and g2-2 is a fixed set of 240 PRs. It tells us if a change to Byte makes it better or worse. It cannot tell us if people act on Byte's findings in real PRs, and that is the point of a reviewer.

G2-10 adds three live numbers. Addressed: a HIGH finding that was dealt with before the merge. Wrong: a finding a person with write access marked with a thumbs-down. Live recall: each month, how many shipped bugs Byte had flagged on the PR that introduced them.

The targets are at least 65% of HIGH findings addressed and under 3% marked wrong. 'Addressed' is counted the way Uber's uReview, its in-house AI reviewer, counts it. So our numbers compare with what others publish.

The weekly-harvest stage of src/weekly.ts already reads merged PRs. G2-10 gives each Byte finding comment on those PRs a fate: one row with ids and enums. The sketch is 25 lines, so it comes in two blocks; nothing is removed between them.
sections.because: We store ids and enums only, so the rows can sit on the telemetry branch without carrying any code or comment text.

notes.text: The privacy rule of every Byte telemetry file: no path, no body. The same rule as runs.jsonl.
A schema number, so a later change to the row can be read side by side with old rows.
The PR and the comment, by number only. Enough to find them again on GitHub.
Byte's severity. null when the finding had none; the dashboards count it as its own group.
The fate: addressed before the merge, or still open at the merge.
wrong is separate from fate. A finding can be addressed and still marked wrong.
When the PR merged, so the nightly job can group rows by week.

p: A finding is addressed in one of two ways. A later sniff called it fulfilled and sure (lesson g2-3). Or GitHub marks the comment outdated at merge: its line is null because the code under it changed. A rebase can also outdate a comment, so the sniff is the stronger signal.
A reply alone does not address anything. Wrong counts only thumbs-downs from write collaborators, people with write access to the repo. The caller filters the reactions and passes the count in.
sections.because: We decide the fate in one small pure function, so the rules can be tested with three fake comments and no GitHub.

notes.text: The two ways a finding counts as addressed, written next to the code that applies them.
Inputs: the GitHub review comment, the sniff verdict for that finding if one exists, and a count.
sniff is undefined when no sniff looked at this finding, for example on a PR with one push.
Only thumbs-downs from writers are counted. The caller does the filtering.
The return type is two fields of FindingFate; the caller fills in the ids.
Outdated: GitHub set line to null but kept original_line, so the comment once had a line.
Fulfilled counts only with sure: a fulfilled verdict below the confidence bar does not.
Either signal makes it addressed. Any writer's thumbs-down makes it wrong.

callout.text: The rows go to finding-fates.jsonl, uploaded as byte-finding-fates-<runId> like the fix fates. The hourly sweep in src/telemetry.ts merges them into data/finding-fates.jsonl, and the G1 nightly job turns them into byte_findings_addressed_ratio{severity,team} and byte_findings_wrong_ratio{team}.

sections.h: Routing, part 1: what counts as small
p: Every review runs at high effort today: CLAUDE_EFFORT in src/limits.ts. Anthropic measured medium matching the old high at about half the tokens. The routing table says low for docs-, test- and dependency-only PRs.

G2-11 adds src/route.ts. reviewRoute(files) returns a model, an effort and a reason. Size is additions plus deletions, with lockfiles and generated files left out, because a 5,000-line package-lock.json says nothing about risk. The sketch is 26 lines, in two blocks with nothing removed.
sections.because: We name the file patterns once at the top, so a reviewer can check what counts as docs, tests or dependencies.

notes.text: The default model stays Opus 5.5. Routing changes the effort, not the reviewer.
PullRequestFile gains additions and deletions in src/types.ts; GitHub already returns them.
Three effort levels used for reviews. The SDK has more, but Byte only routes between these.
Above 400 changed lines, a PR keeps today's high effort.
Lockfiles and generated gRPC stubs (_pb2.py and .pyi). They never count towards size.
Docs: Markdown and text files, and anything under a docs/ folder.
Tests: test folders, *.test.ts and *.spec.ts files, and Python test_*.py files.
Dependencies: package.json, pyproject.toml and requirements files.

p: The function filters out generated files and adds up the lines. Then it asks one question per kind: is every remaining file of this kind? A PR that is only docs, only tests or only dependencies gets low. A big PR keeps high, and everything else gets medium.

The gate calls reviewRoute() where it resolves the model today, and a team model set in policy still wins. A new effort gate output reaches review.yml, which passes --effort "$EFFORT". cli.ts reads it as optional, with CLAUDE_EFFORT as the default, and engines.ts uses it instead of the constant.

Each route must earn its place. On its BYTE-GOLD dev slice, HIGH recall must stay within 3 points of today's high. False alarms on clean PRs must not rise. A route that loses goes back to high, and the change ships through the G2-09 gate.
sections.because: We route on facts GitHub gives us, size and file kinds, so the choice is repeatable and shows its reason.

notes.text: Input: the PR's files with their line counts. Output: model, effort and a reason for the status comment.
Drop lockfiles and generated stubs first, so they affect neither size nor kind.
Changed lines: additions plus deletions over the files that count.
A small helper: true when every counted file matches the pattern.
All docs, all tests or all dependencies: the cheapest route.
Big PRs keep today's high effort. The reason names the line count.
Everything else: medium, which Anthropic measured close to the old high.

callout.text: G2-11 also adds claude-sonnet-5-5 to SUPPORTED_MODELS, for the panel's conventions lens later. Reviews themselves stay on Opus 5.5; only the effort moves.

sections.h: Risk labels, part 1: tiers live in Byte's policy
p: With exactly one approval per PR, the reviewer needs to know which PRs touch migrations, permissions or the cloud-client contract. G2-12 gives every fcp PR a label, risk:low, risk:med or risk:high, with the reason in a check named Byte risk. It tells the reviewer where to look. It never changes who may approve or how many approvals are needed.

The tiers live in Byte's config/repositories.json, as a risk block per repository. Policy is baked into Byte's signed image and never read from the reviewed repo, so a PR cannot lower its own tier. The sketch is 30 lines, in two blocks with nothing removed.
sections.because: We keep the tier rules out of fcp, because any file in fcp is a file a PR to fcp can change.

notes.text: isPathAllowed is Byte's existing glob matcher from src/policy.ts. The tiers reuse it.
Where the rules live: the repository's entry in config/repositories.json, inside the signed image.
High-risk globs with one reason, for example migrations: a schema change.
Low-risk globs: docs, stories and tests only.
Anything no rule claims is med. That is the default, not a third list.
A rule is a list of globs and the reason shown to the reviewer.
Above 800 changed lines, a PR goes up one tier.
The order used to go up one step: low, then med, then high.

callout.text: fcp's draft high list comes from the BE and FE guilds. It holds rhinoCore migrations and permissions.py, both rhinoAgentRpc folders, frontend auth routes and the API auth folder. It also holds frontend/src/proxy.ts and .github/workflows. Low is docs, stories and tests only.

p: riskFor starts at low if every file is low, else med. One high file makes the PR high. Then size can raise the tier one step. If nothing matched, the reason still says why the PR got its tier.

A new risk subcommand in src/cli.ts lists the PR's files with the read token and calls riskFor. It sets the one label and removes the other two. Then it creates a completed check run, Byte risk, with conclusion neutral and the matched rules. A neutral check shows information and is neither green nor red.

fcp gets a new caller, .github/workflows/byte-risk.yml, on pull_request opened, reopened, synchronize and ready_for_review. It is not added to byte-review.yml, because adding opened there would start a full review on every new PR. The check is never added to the ruleset.
sections.because: We compute the tier in a pure function over file names and line counts, so tests need no GitHub.

notes.text: Inputs: the files and the repository's risk policy. Output: a tier and the reasons.
Low only when a low rule exists and every file matches it. Otherwise med.
The files that match a high glob, or none when the policy has no high rule.
One high-risk file is enough for the whole PR to be high.
The reason says how many files and why, for example 1 file(s): schema change.
Lines are counted over all files here, unlike reviewRoute.
Go up one step in ORDER. High is already the top, so it never moves.
Always return at least one reason, so the check run is never empty.

callout.text: The label informs the one reviewer. It never adds or removes an approval and is never a required check. Every PR keeps exactly one approval, never by the requester.

sections.h: Deep mode only where a miss hurts
p: The panel from lesson g2-5 runs five review lenses and a skeptic. Anthropic's multi-agent review costs about $15-25 a PR at list price, against about $2 for Byte today. G2-17 runs it only on risk:high PRs, PRs over 800 changed lines, or when someone comments @byte-review deep.

Before widening it, W10 measures it. Replay the BYTE-GOLD dev split in both modes. Compare HIGH recall, precision, clean false alarms, cost and minutes per PR, per lens. Deep mode ships for risk:high only if HIGH recall is not lower and clean false alarms stay at most 0.2 per PR.

Widening it to more PRs, or making the panel the default, is Sean and Nave's call from those numbers. Runs are tagged mode: deep in data/runs.jsonl, and the result goes into Byte's ROADMAP.md with what would change the decision.
sections.because: We decide the mode from the tier and the size the gate already has, so the choice costs nothing and explains itself.

notes.text: Only the type is imported: the tier itself comes from riskFor(), called in the gate.
Two modes. Standard is today's single CLAUDE_BUILTIN session.
The same 800-line line as the risk raise, so big PRs get both.
asked is set when the command parser reads deep after @byte-review: a mode, not a team.
A person asking wins over every other rule.
risk:high gets the panel, the case the W10 numbers must justify.
Very large PRs also get the panel.
Everything else stays on the single session.

quiz.q: A PR changes 3 Markdown files and frontend/package-lock.json with 4,000 changed lines. Which effort does reviewRoute pick?

options.text: high, because the PR has more than 400 changed lines
options.why: The lockfile matches GENERATED and is dropped before counting.

options.text: low: the lockfile is left out, and every remaining file is docs
options.why: counted holds only the three Markdown files, so all(DOCS) is true.

options.text: medium, because the files are of mixed kinds
options.why: Kinds are checked after generated files are removed; nothing mixed is left.

quiz.q: Why do fcp's risk tiers live in Byte's config/repositories.json and not in a file inside fcp?

options.text: So the risk label can be added to the ruleset as a required check
options.why: The check is never added to the ruleset; it only informs the reviewer.

options.text: Because JSON loads faster than YAML in a GitHub Action
options.why: Speed is not the reason. The question is who can change the rules.

options.text: Policy is baked into Byte's signed image and never read from the reviewed repo, so a PR cannot lower its own tier
options.why: Any file in fcp is a file a PR to fcp can edit.

quiz.q: A Byte comment sits on a line the author later rewrote. At merge, GitHub shows it as outdated. Nobody replied. What fate does it get?

options.text: addressed: its line is null because the code under it changed
options.why: Outdated at merge is one of the two addressed signals; a reply is not needed.

options.text: open, because nobody replied to it
options.why: Replies do not count either way; the code change does.

options.text: wrong, because the author ignored it
options.why: wrong counts only thumbs-downs from writers.

From p8-8: what is effort, and why does changing it per message keep the prompt cache warm?

words.plain: One row per Byte finding on a merged PR: addressed or open, and wrong or not. Ids and enums only.
A finding a sure sniff called fulfilled, or whose comment GitHub marked outdated at merge.
Each month, the share of shipped bugs that Byte had flagged on the PR that introduced them.
The model, effort and reason Byte picks for one review from the PR's size and kind.
risk:low, risk:med or risk:high, set from path rules in Byte's policy and the PR's size.
A completed check run that shows information without passing or failing the PR.
The panel review (five lenses and a skeptic), used for risk:high, big PRs or @byte-review deep.
